title: Boss: text that is not what it seems
summary: Reports that grep calls binary, a search that finds nothing, and a bulk rename that would have destroyed every photo name. Diagnose each from its symptom and fix it.

steps.title: Ticket OPS-2310
body: *"Three things from this week: (1) the Linux alerting job says the ops reports have no ERROR lines, but I can see
them; (2) the price-error counter says 0 and support says there were dozens; (3) before I run the photo rename on the
marketing share, can someone check it? The dry run looks odd."*
All three are about text: how it is stored, how it is quoted, how a pattern is read. Start from what you can see.

steps.title: grep: binary file matches
prompt: The alerting job runs `grep -c ERROR ~/reports/*.txt`. Run it (yes, `grep` works here: it is a native program).
Then compare with `Select-String -Path ~/reports/*.txt -Pattern ERROR`, and look at the first bytes:
Convert **every** `.txt` file in `~/reports` **in place** to UTF-8 without a BOM, so `grep -c ERROR` counts 2 in

checks.name: grep counts the errors
checks.fail: `grep -c ERROR` should find 1 line in `daily.txt` and 2 in `weekly.txt`.

checks.name: plain UTF-8, no BOM, text intact
checks.cmd: for f in ~/reports/*.txt; do head -c2 "$f" | od -An -tx1 | grep -Eq 'ff fe|ef bb' && echo "$f still has a BOM"; done; tr -d '\r' < ~/reports/weekly.txt | sed -n 4p
checks.fail: The files should start with the text itself (no `FF FE` or `EF BB BF` bytes), and `weekly.txt` line 4 should read `ERROR disk 91% on fs02`.

hints: `FF FE` at the start means UTF-16 LE: every character takes two bytes, half of them zero, so grep sees a binary file. Windows PowerShell 5.1's `>` writes exactly this.
PowerShell 7's `Get-Content` reads the BOM and decodes UTF-16 correctly; its `Set-Content` writes UTF-8 without a BOM.
Read the whole file before writing it: `Get-ChildItem ~/reports -Filter *.txt | ForEach-Object { $text = Get-Content -LiteralPath $_.FullName; Set-Content -LiteralPath $_.FullName -Value $text }`
explain: `Get-Content x | Set-Content x` in one pipeline can wipe the file: `Set-Content` opens it for writing while lines are
still being read. Read into a variable (or wrap in parentheses: `(Get-Content x) | Set-Content x`) first. The
lasting fix is upstream: make the 5.1 job write `-Encoding utf8`, or run it in `pwsh`.

steps.title: Zero price errors?
prompt: `pwsh -File ~/scripts/count-price-errors.ps1` says `total 0`. Support counted many rejections with the message
Fix the script so it prints one `<file> <count>` line per log and the right `total N`.

checks.name: the right total
checks.fail: The last line should be `total N` with the real count.

checks.name: per-file counts match grep
checks.cmd: diff <(pwsh -NoProfile -File ~/scripts/count-price-errors.ps1 | tr -d '\r' | sort) <( (cd ~/logs && grep -F -c 'price: $5.00 (USD)' *.log | tr ':' ' '; echo "total $(cat ~/logs/*.log | grep -F -c 'price: $5.00 (USD)')") | sort)
checks.fail: The script's counts should match `grep -F -c 'price: $5.00 (USD)'` per file, plus the total.

hints: Two separate things go wrong with `"price: $5.00 (USD)"`. Print the string on its own first: `"price: $5.00 (USD)"`.
In double quotes `$5` is a variable (empty), so the pattern became `price: .00 (USD)`. And even with single quotes, `-Pattern` is a regex: `$`, `.`, `(` and `)` mean something there.
steps.explain: Rule of thumb: single quotes for anything that is not meant to expand, and `-SimpleMatch` (or `[regex]::Escape($text)`) when searching for text a user or a log gave you. `Set-StrictMode -Version Latest` at the top would have caught the first half: reading the never-set variable `$5` becomes an error instead of an empty string.

steps.title: The rename dry run looks odd
prompt: Run `pwsh -File ~/scripts/rename-photos.ps1`. It has `-WhatIf`, so nothing changes yet. Read the new names it
Fix the script, check the dry run again, then make it do the rename for real: every `IMG_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS.jpg` in
`~/photos` becomes `YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS.jpg`. `cover.png` must stay as it is.

checks.name: contents untouched
checks.fail: Each file should keep its own contents: rename, do not copy or recreate.

checks.name: the script uses a literal replacement
checks.fail: The replacement in the script should be `'$1-$2-$3_$4'` in single quotes, so the next run is right too.

hints: The dry run shows the target as `--.jpg`... In double quotes, what are `$1`, `$2` and `$3_` to PowerShell?
They are variables, expanded (to nothing) before `-replace` runs. Single quotes pass `$1` through to the regex engine.
Change `"$1-$2-$3_$4"` to `'$1-$2-$3_$4'`, run the dry run, then remove ` -WhatIf` and run it again.
explain: Without the dry run, all four photos would have been renamed to the same `--.jpg`: the first rename wins and the
other three fail with *Cannot create a file when that file already exists*, or worse, on a tool that overwrites.
